name: l01-uid-gid
title: The kernel compares numbers
spec: Left box: a process, labelled 'runs as UID and GID'. Right box: a file, labelled 'owner, group and permission bits'. A central green box 'kernel compares the numbers' with arrows from both sides, leading to 'allow or deny'. Below, an orange chip: root has UID 0 and bypasses most permission checks. Green takeaway bar: the kernel enforces access on numbers, not names.
alt: A process with a UID and GID and a file with owner and permission bits are compared by the kernel.
cap: The kernel decides access by comparing the numeric IDs of the process with the owner, group and permission bits on the file.

name: l01-asymmetry
title: Kernel and user space move independently
spec: Two stacked layers: top 'user space (glibc, programs)', bottom 'kernel'. Left panel green: 'old user-space binary on newer kernel' with a check mark, label 'works: never break user space'. Right panel two orange failures: 'program built against newer glibc on older distribution: fails to start' and 'kernel module (.ko) built for one kernel build on another: refuses to load'. Bottom bar: Standardise a single tested OS release across every node.
alt: Old programs run on new kernels, but newer glibc programs and kernel modules fail on mismatched systems.
cap: Kernel and user space move independently, and the reverse direction fails in two ways.

name: l01-layer-failures
title: Which layer does the failure live in
spec: Table with three columns: Symptom, Layer, First check. Rows: 'nvidia-smi fails after kernel update' | kernel modules | uname -r ; 'GLIBC_2.xx not found' | user-space libraries | ldd ./binary ; 'kill -9 has no effect, state D' | kernel waiting on hardware | dmesg ; 'Out of memory: Killed process' | kernel OOM killer | memory.max ; 'ENOENT versus EACCES' | system call return code | strace. Commands in monospace. Orange highlight on the Layer column header.
anchor: ## 8. How it fails: six classic confusions
alt: A table mapping six classic failure symptoms to the system layer that causes them.
cap: Before touching anything, ask which layer of the system the failure actually lives in.

name: l02-command-anatomy
title: Anatomy of a command line
spec: Large monospace line: ls -l -a /var/log. Four labelled callouts with arrows: 'ls' command, '-l' option, '-a' option, '/var/log' argument (what to act on). Below, small list of conventions: -l short option, --all long option, -n 20 option with value, -- end of options with example rm -- -weird-file. Orange highlight on '--'.
alt: A command line split into command, options and argument.
cap: A command line is a command, its options and its arguments.

name: l02-path-lookup
title: How the shell finds a bare word
spec: Vertical flow of four boxes, top to bottom, for typing python3: 'alias' then 'function' then 'builtin' then 'PATH directories searched in order'. Arrow out of the last box to 'program runs'. Side panel with monospace commands: type -a python3 (every way it could resolve, in order); command -v python3 (the one that will run). Orange note: wrong version runs, check PATH order or an alias first.
anchor: ### How the shell finds a program: `PATH`
alt: A bare command name is looked up as alias, function, builtin and then each PATH directory.
cap: The shell checks aliases, functions and builtins before searching PATH in order.

name: l02-chaining
title: Combining commands
spec: Table with two columns, Form and Runs the second command when. Rows: a ; b | always, after a ends ; a && b | a succeeded (status 0) ; a || b | a failed (status non-zero) ; a & b | a started in background, b runs immediately ; (a; b) | in a subshell ; { a; b; } | as a group in the current shell. Forms in monospace. Green bar example: mkdir -p build && cd build && cmake .. stops at the first failure.
alt: A table of the ways to chain commands and when the second one runs.
cap: Operators decide whether the second command runs based on the first command's exit status.

name: l03-fhs-tree
title: The standard layout
spec: Tree rooted at '/' with children as boxes, each with a short purpose: /etc system-wide configuration (plain text); /var variable data (/var/log, /var/lib); /usr bulk of installed software (/usr/bin, /usr/lib, /usr/local); /home users' personal files; /tmp temporary files; /run runtime data since boot; /dev device files; /proc and /sys virtual, generated by the kernel (orange); /boot kernel image and initramfs; /opt third-party software. Side note: /bin, /sbin, /lib are symbolic links into /usr. Paths in monospace.
anchor: ## 2. The standard layout: where things live
alt: The root directory with its standard subdirectories and what each one holds.
cap: The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard tells you where each kind of file lives on every Linux machine.

name: l03-ls-columns
title: Reading one ls -l line
spec: One monospace line: -rw-r--r-- 1 juser users 3804 May 28 10:40 abusive.c. Callouts below, in order: file type and permissions; hard link count (1); owner (juser); group (users); size in bytes (3804); modification date and time; file name. Orange highlight on the first column. Small note: ls -F appends a mark to each name.
anchor: ### Reading a long listing column by column
alt: One ls -l line with each column labelled.
cap: Each column of a long listing answers one question about the file.

name: l03-deleted-open
title: Deleted but still open
spec: Left: df shows 95% used. Right: du -sh /* totals much less. Between them a flow: a large log is deleted while a process still has it open, the name is gone, the space is not, until the process closes the file or exits. Diagnose box in monospace: sudo lsof +L1. Orange mark on 'the name is gone, but the space is not'.
anchor: ### 4. The disk is full, but `du` cannot find the files: deleted but still open
alt: A deleted file that a process still holds open keeps using disk space that du cannot see.
cap: df counts the space while a process holds the file open, but du no longer finds the name.

name: l04-regex-map
title: Regex metacharacters
spec: Grid of labelled cells, monospace pattern then meaning: . any single character; * zero or more of the preceding item; + one or more (extended); ? zero or one (extended); ^ start of line; $ end of line; [abc] one of the set; [^abc] not in the set; {n,m} n to m repetitions; \. a literal dot. Orange note: . matches exactly one arbitrary character, and .* is greedy.
alt: A grid of common regular expression metacharacters and what each matches.
cap: Most characters match themselves, and a small set of metacharacters carries special meaning.

name: l04-bre-ere
title: BRE versus ERE
spec: Two columns. Left, BRE (default in grep and sed): + ? | () { } are literal text unless preceded by a backslash. Right, ERE (grep -E, sed -E, awk): the same characters are operators straight away, a literal plus needs a backslash. Bottom row of tools: GNU grep -P enables Perl-compatible expressions, not on macOS grep. Green bar: use -E unless you have a reason not to.
alt: Basic and extended regular expressions treat plus, question mark, pipe, parentheses and braces oppositely.
cap: BRE treats those characters as literal unless escaped, while ERE treats them as operators.

name: l04-sed-substitute
title: Anatomy of sed substitute
spec: Large monospace line: sed 's/old/new/g' file. Labels: s substitute command, old pattern, new replacement, g all matches on each line (without g only the first), file input. Below three small rows: sed -E 's/step=([0-9]+)/STEP:\1/' file with note \1 is the first capture group; sed 's|/usr/local|/opt|g' file other delimiter; sed -n '10,20p' file prints lines 10 to 20. Orange note: sed writes to standard output, -i edits the file in place.
alt: The parts of a sed substitute command with a few variations.
cap: sed applies an edit to each line as it passes through and does not change the file unless asked.

name: l05-copy-tools
title: Which copy tool for which goal
spec: Table with Goal then Tool. Rows: one-off copy of a file or two | scp ; interactive browsing | sftp host ; keep directory trees in step | rsync (highlighted orange: transfers only differences, preserves permissions, resumable) ; stream a tree with no temporary archive | tar | ssh ; mount remote directory | sshfs host:/path mnt ; share among Linux machines | NFS ; share with Windows | Samba ; cloud object stores | rclone, gcloud storage, aws s3. Tools in monospace.
alt: A goal-to-tool table for copying files over SSH and the network.
cap: A one-off copy suits scp, while a directory you keep in step suits rsync.

name: l05-fanout
title: Running one command on many nodes
spec: Left: one box 'your terminal'. Arrows fan out to a column of nodes gpu01, gpu02 ... gpu16. Four tool chips with monospace example: pdsh -w gpu[01-16] with dshbak -c ; clush -w gpu[01-16] -b ; srun -N16 --ntasks-per-node=1 hostname ; ansible gpu -m shell. Right: identical outputs gathered into one line, one outlier node highlighted orange. Note: node ranges like gpu[01-16].
alt: One terminal fans a command out to many nodes and the identical outputs are grouped.
cap: A healthy fleet prints one grouped line, so an outlier node stands out.

name: l05-bmc
title: Out-of-band access
spec: Two paths into one server. Top path, green, 'SSH over the OS network' ending at 'operating system', marked blocked when the OS has crashed or the network is broken. Bottom path, orange, 'BMC (baseboard management controller)' with its own network port and IP address, works even when the main system is powered off. Monospace examples: ipmitool ... chassis power status ; sol activate ; chassis power cycle. Note: BMC network must be isolated.
anchor: ## 8. Out-of-band access: when SSH is not available
alt: The BMC gives a second way into a server when SSH and the operating system are unavailable.
cap: The BMC has its own network port and works even when the main system is powered off.

name: l05-hpc-path
title: The standard HPC path
spec: Horizontal chain: laptop, bastion, Slurm login node, compute node. Last arrow labelled srun --pty bash or salloc (monospace). Orange note under the last arrow: do not ssh into compute nodes uninvited; processes started outside Slurm are not tracked by it.
alt: From laptop through a bastion and login node to a compute node using srun or salloc.
cap: On an HPC cluster you reach a compute node through Slurm rather than by logging in directly.

name: l06-passwd-line
title: One line of /etc/passwd
spec: Monospace line: alice:x:1042:1042:Alice Example,Room 12:/home/alice:/bin/bash. Seven callouts in order: login name; x password marker (hash is in /etc/shadow); UID 1042; GID 1042 of primary group; GECOS comment; home directory /home/alice; login shell /bin/bash. Orange note: an empty password field means no password is required, never expected.
alt: A passwd line split into its seven colon-separated fields.
cap: Each passwd line has seven fields: name, password marker, UID, GID, comment, home and shell.

name: l06-setuid-ids
title: Real versus effective UID
spec: Two-row diagram. Row 1: you run a normal program: ruid = you, euid = you. Row 2: you run a setuid program owned by root: ruid stays yours (green), euid becomes the file owner's (orange). Legend: euid is the identity used for permission checks (the actor); ruid is who started the process and who may signal it (the owner); saved UID lets euid switch back. Monospace: ps -eo pid,euser,ruser,comm.
alt: A setuid program keeps your real UID while its effective UID becomes the file owner.
cap: The effective UID is used for permission checks while the real UID records who started the process.

name: l06-acl
title: Beyond owner, group and other
spec: Left box 'classic permissions': owner, group, other. Right box 'ACL adds named entries': u:alice:rw, u:bob:rw, g:readers:r. Between them a box 'mask caps effective permission of the extra entries'. Below: 'default ACL (setfacl -d) is inherited by new files and subdirectories'. Monospace chips: setfacl -m u:alice:rw mydir ; getfacl mydir ; ls -l shows a + at the end of the permissions. Orange highlight on the mask.
alt: ACLs add named user and group entries on top of owner, group and other, limited by a mask.
cap: An ACL lets you grant specific users or groups access without changing the owner or group.

name: l07-package-anatomy
title: What is inside a package
spec: One large box labelled 'package (one file)'. Inside two parts: 'tree of files' and 'metadata' listing: name, version, architecture; dependencies; file checksums; marked configuration files; maintainer scripts; signature. Each metadata item with a short arrow to what it enables: searching and refusing the wrong architecture; tool installs everything else needed; verify nothing altered; upgrades keep your edits; creates user or enables service; proof it came from the repository owner.
alt: A package holds a tree of files plus metadata that enables dependencies, verification and safe upgrades.
cap: The metadata is what lets the tool install dependencies, verify files and keep your edits.

name: l07-verbs
title: Same task, two families
spec: Table with Task, Debian family, Red Hat family. Rows: refresh metadata | sudo apt update | sudo dnf makecache ; install | sudo apt install pkg1 pkg2 | sudo dnf install pkg1 pkg2 ; remove | sudo apt remove pkg | sudo dnf remove pkg ; upgrade | sudo apt upgrade | sudo dnf upgrade ; search | apt search word | dnf search word ; show details | apt show pkg | dnf info pkg ; which version would be used | apt policy pkg | dnf list --showduplicates pkg. All commands monospace. Debian column and Red Hat column in two shades of green.
anchor: ### Verbs you need on both sides
alt: A translation table of everyday package commands between the Debian and Red Hat families.
cap: Most day-to-day package tasks have a matching command in each family.

name: l07-loader-search
title: How the loader finds a library
spec: Numbered vertical list of four search steps with arrows downward: 1 the executable's embedded RPATH or RUNPATH; 2 the LD_LIBRARY_PATH environment variable; 3 the cache /etc/ld.so.cache built from /etc/ld.so.conf (rebuilt by sudo ldconfig); 4 default directories /lib and /usr/lib. Side box: ldd /bin/bash shows what the program asked for on the left of the arrow and where it was found on the right; 'libfoo.so.1 => not found' is the problem (orange). Names in monospace.
alt: The four places the dynamic loader searches, in order, for a shared library.
cap: The loader checks RPATH, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, the ld.so cache and then the default directories.

name: l08-zombie-orphan
title: Zombies and orphans
spec: Two panels. Panel 1 Zombie: child process exits, releases memory and files, leaves a process-table entry holding the exit status until the parent calls wait(); label 'uses no CPU or memory, cannot be killed, fix is to make the parent wait()'. Panel 2 Orphan: parent exits before child, child is re-parented to PID 1 or a subreaper which must wait() for it (orange). Footer note: in a container, PID 1 that never reaps children leaves permanent zombies; fix with a tiny init such as tini.
alt: A zombie is an exited child waiting for its parent to collect the status, and an orphan is reparented to PID 1.
cap: A zombie holds only a PID slot until the parent calls wait(), and orphans are adopted by PID 1.

name: l08-load-average
title: Reading the load average
spec: Left: run queue box with tasks waiting for cores, plus a D-state (waiting for I/O) group that also counts. Right decision list: compare with nproc; load below the thread count means not all cores are busy; load stays above means tasks are queuing; high load with idle CPUs (orange) means tasks stuck waiting for I/O, check vmstat b column, wa, and iostat; high load with sluggish system points to memory pressure and swapping or I/O. Green bar: if you see a high load with idle CPUs, look at I/O first.
anchor: ### The run queue and the load average
alt: Load average counts running, runnable and uninterruptible tasks, so compare it with CPU count and check I/O.
cap: A high load with idle CPUs means many tasks are stuck waiting for I/O.

name: l08-proc-pid
title: What lives in /proc/PID
spec: Central folder box /proc/PID with spokes to short labelled files: status (name, state, UIDs, VmRSS); cmdline; environ; cwd, exe, root (symlinks); fd/ (one symlink per open descriptor); maps and smaps (memory mappings); limits; io (read_bytes, write_bytes); wchan and stack (kernel function waiting in); cgroup; ns/. Monospace names. Separate small box: system-wide /proc/loadavg, /proc/meminfo, /proc/pressure/*. Orange note: reading these is how ps and top work.
anchor: ### `/proc`: the kernel's window on every process
alt: Each process has a /proc directory whose files expose its state, memory, files and limits.
cap: Reading /proc files is how ps and top work, and you can read them yourself.

name: l08-hangup-remedies
title: Keeping a job alive after disconnect
spec: Top: SSH session drops, shell gets SIGHUP and forwards it to its jobs, job terminates (orange). Below: five remedies as boxes: tmux or screen; submit to the scheduler (sbatch, a Kubernetes Job); nohup ./run.sh > run.log 2>&1 &; disown -h after Ctrl-Z and bg; a systemd service or timer. Mark tmux as best for interactive, scheduler as right answer for anything that matters. Green bar: pick the remedy before you start the job, not after the connection drops.
alt: Dropping the SSH session sends SIGHUP to jobs, and five remedies keep work alive.
cap: Choose tmux, the scheduler, nohup, disown or systemd before the connection drops.

name: l09-run-source
title: Run, source or exec
spec: Table with How, What happens, Variables visible afterwards. Rows: ./script.sh | new child process | No ; source script.sh or . script.sh | current shell executes the commands | Yes (green highlight) ; exec ./script.sh | replaces the current shell | shell no longer exists ; bash -x script.sh | run with tracing | No. Commands in monospace. Note: a child cannot change its parent's environment.
alt: Running, sourcing and exec differ in whether the script's variables survive in your shell.
cap: Only sourcing leaves the script's variables in your current shell.

name: l09-args
title: The three argument loops
spec: Script called as: script 'abc 123' qwe. Three rows each showing loop and output: for a in "$@" gives [abc 123] [qwe] (green, correct); for a in $@ gives [abc] [123] [qwe] (orange, broken); for a in "$*" gives [abc 123 qwe] one word. Loops in monospace. Note: "$*" joins with the first character of IFS.
alt: Three ways of looping over arguments and what each one produces.
cap: Quoted dollar-at keeps each argument as one word, while the other forms split or join them.

name: l09-subshell
title: Subshell versus group
spec: Two panels. Left (commands ) subshell: child copy of the shell, example myvar=10 then ( myvar=20 ); echo gives 10, changes vanish. Right { commands; } current shell: myvar=30 then echo gives 30; note the spaces and semicolon; use for one redirection: { echo a; echo b; } > file. Footer orange: each stage of a pipeline runs in its own subshell, so echo hi | read x; echo "$x" prints nothing. Code in monospace.
alt: A subshell discards its changes, while a brace group runs in the current shell.
cap: Changes made inside a subshell vanish when it ends, but a brace group changes the current shell.

name: l09-retry
title: Retry with backoff
spec: Loop diagram: run command; success then done; failure then 'attempts left?' If no, 'failed after n attempts' exit 1 (orange). If yes, sleep delay then delay doubles, back to run. Side box monospace: retry 5 2 curl -fsS https://example.com/file -o /tmp/file ; timeout 30 ssh -o ConnectTimeout=5 -o BatchMode=yes node01 true. Green bar: always put a timeout on anything that can block.
alt: A retry loop that sleeps with a doubling delay until the attempts run out.
cap: Retries with a growing delay and a timeout keep scripts from hanging or failing on transient errors.

name: l10-device-types
title: Reading a device listing
spec: Monospace lines: brw-rw---- 1 root disk 8, 1 ... /dev/sda1 ; crw-rw-rw- 1 root root 1, 3 ... /dev/null ; crw-rw-rw- 1 root root 195, 0 ... /dev/nvidia0 ; prw-r--r-- ... /run/fifo ; srw-rw-rw- ... /dev/log. Callout on the first character: b block device (disks, partitions), c character device (stream of bytes: /dev/null, GPUs), p named pipe, s Unix domain socket. Callout on '8, 1': major number selects the driver (the building), minor number selects the instance (the room). Note: /proc/devices lists drivers and major numbers.
alt: How the first letter and the major and minor numbers of an ls -l line identify a device.
cap: The type letter and the major and minor numbers tell you what kind of device a file is.

name: l10-name-shift
title: Why sdX names are a trap
spec: Two columns Before and After a reboot. Before: sda, sdb, sdc. After sdb fails: sda, sdb (was sdc). Arrow from old sdc to new sdb in orange, label 'the name moved, nothing broke inside the filesystem'. Bottom green row of stable identifiers: UUID=... in fstab, /dev/mapper/vg-lv, /dev/disk/by-id (physical drive by serial), /dev/disk/by-path (slot), /dev/disk/by-uuid (recommended fstab key); GPUs by UUID from nvidia-smi -L. Paths in monospace.
anchor: ### Naming: why enumeration order is a trap
alt: Kernel disk names can shift between boots, so persistent configuration should use stable identifiers.
cap: Names like sdb depend on discovery order, so use a UUID or a /dev/disk link instead.

name: l10-driver-bind
title: Binding a device to a driver
spec: Flow: device ID (PCI vendor and device pair) then modalias then udev loads matching module then driver claims device. Side box of sysfs commands in monospace: readlink /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:3b:00.0/driver ; ls /sys/bus/pci/drivers/nvidia. Lower row, orange illustrative swap to VFIO: unbind from current driver, set driver_override to vfio-pci, drivers_probe. Note: drain the node before any of these operations.
alt: A device is matched to a driver by its ID tables, and sysfs can unbind it and hand it to vfio-pci.
cap: Drivers claim devices by ID, and the bind and unbind files in sysfs let you swap the driver.

name: l11-lib-names
title: Three names for one library
spec: Three stacked rows, each a box with a role label. libfoo.so | linker name | used at BUILD time (-lfoo), usually a symlink, shipped in the -dev package. libfoo.so.1 | soname | recorded in programs that link against it (DT_NEEDED), the compatibility contract (orange). libfoo.so.1.2.3 | real name | the actual file. Arrows from linker name to soname to real name labelled symlinks. Note: the number in the soname is the ABI version, so a bug-fix release 1.2.4 can replace 1.2.3 without relinking. Names monospace.
anchor: ### Names: soname, real name, linker name
alt: A shared library has a linker name, a soname and a real file name tied together by symlinks.
cap: Programs record the soname, which is the compatibility contract, while the real name is the actual file.

name: l11-glibc-direction
title: Binaries and glibc versions
spec: Two hosts side by side. Left: build host with newer glibc, binary built there. Right: older distribution with older glibc. Arrow from left to right in orange with error text in monospace: version `GLIBC_2.34' not found (required by ./prog). Reverse arrow green: build on the oldest distribution you intend to support, runs on newer. Lower box with two commands: objdump -T ./prog | grep -o 'GLIBC_[0-9.]*' | sort -Vu | tail -1 (what the binary needs) ; ldd --version (what the system offers). Takeaway bar: binaries are forward-compatible with newer glibc, not backward.
alt: A binary built against a newer glibc fails on an older system, but not the other way round.
cap: Binaries are forward-compatible with newer glibc, not backward, so build on the oldest distribution you support.

name: l11-strace-reading
title: Reading a strace by symptom
spec: Table with Symptom, What to look for, Command. Rows: cannot find config | last failed openat before the error, ENOENT or EACCES | grep -n 'ENOENT\|EACCES' /tmp/t.out ; which library loaded | openat lines for .so files | grep openat /tmp/t.out | grep '\.so' ; hung | futex(..., FUTEX_WAIT...) waiting on a lock; epoll_wait or poll waiting for events | strace -p PID ; slow | counts per call type, many small reads or many failed stat | strace -c -f -p PID. Commands monospace. Orange note: strace stops the target at every system call, so it adds overhead.
anchor: ## 6. Watching a program: `strace` and `ltrace` in practice
alt: A table that maps common symptoms to what to look for in a strace output.
cap: Read a trace with one question in mind and use the matching filter or summary flag.

name: l12-attach-paths
title: How storage is attached
spec: Five rows from simple to shared, each a box with a one-line note: Disk devices (JBOD) the OS sees each disk, easiest to observe; RAID controller or software groups disks into one virtual disk, hardware RAID hides physical disks from the OS; Storage arrays and SANs behind controllers with big caches, attach by FC, SAS or iSCSI, often multipath; NAS over NFS, SMB/CIFS or iSCSI, the network becomes part of the I/O path; Local NVMe in GPU servers for scratch data, caches, fast checkpoints, belongs to that one machine (orange: on the cloud an instance restart can lose it).
alt: Five ways a disk can reach a system and what each one changes about what you can see.
cap: How storage is attached decides what you can see and what you can control.

name: l12-fs-types
title: Choosing a filesystem type
spec: Table with Type, Character, Note for AI nodes. Rows: ext4 | Linux default for years | reliable general purpose ; XFS | allocation groups for parallel allocation, online grow, cannot shrink | default on RHEL family, big files and parallel I/O ; btrfs | copy-on-write, subvolumes, snapshots | use with care for databases ; ZFS | volume manager plus filesystem, ARC cache | out-of-tree, memory-hungry ARC ; tmpfs | in memory | /run, /dev/shm ; overlayfs | lower read-only layers plus upper writable | container root filesystems ; NFS, Lustre, GPFS, BeeGFS, CephFS | network and parallel | shared datasets and checkpoints. Footer: the kernel VFS layer lets them all coexist under one tree.
alt: A comparison table of the common Linux filesystem types and where each fits.
cap: The VFS layer lets many different filesystems coexist under one directory tree.

name: l12-atomic-replace
title: Replacing a file safely
spec: Four numbered boxes in a row with arrows: 1 write a temporary file in the same directory; 2 fsync it; 3 rename() it over the target; 4 fsync the directory. Above, orange contrast: a normal write() copies data into the page cache and returns, the data is not durable yet; flusher threads write dirty pages later. Note below: even then, a device write cache can still hold data. Code names in monospace.
alt: The four-step pattern for replacing a file atomically and durably.
cap: A normal write is not durable until flushed, so careful code writes, fsyncs, renames and fsyncs the directory.

name: l13-cloud-grow
title: The disk grew: grow every layer
spec: Vertical stack of five layers with arrows pointing up, each with its command: cloud disk resized in console, then kernel rescan: echo 1 | sudo tee /sys/class/block/sdb/device/rescan ; partition: sudo growpart /dev/sdb 1 ; PV: sudo pvresize /dev/sdb1 ; LV plus filesystem: sudo lvextend -r -l +100%FREE /dev/myvg/mylv1. Green bar: work up the stack one layer at a time. Orange highlight on the first layer: the machine does not notice until you tell it.
anchor: ### Cloud pattern: the disk grew, grow everything above it
alt: Growing a resized cloud disk requires growing the partition, PV, LV and filesystem in order.
cap: Work up the stack one layer at a time: disk, partition, physical volume, then logical volume and filesystem.

name: l13-thin-pool
title: Thin provisioning
spec: One box 'thin pool tp (500G)' in the middle. Above it three virtual volumes, vol1 200G and two more, whose total size is larger than the pool (over-provisioning). Space used only as data is written. A cheap thin snapshot vol1snap, needs no size. Commands monospace: lvcreate -L 500G --thinpool tp myvg ; lvcreate -V 200G --thin -n vol1 myvg/tp ; lvs -a -o +data_percent,metadata_percent. Orange warning: a thin pool that reaches 100% data or metadata corrupts or blocks the volumes in it, watch Data% and Meta%.
alt: Several virtual volumes share one thin pool whose total size can be exceeded by the volumes.
cap: A thin pool that reaches 100% corrupts or blocks the volumes in it, so monitor it.

name: l13-raid-choice
title: Which RAID for what
spec: Table with Purpose, Typical choice, Reason. Rows: Operating system | RAID 1 across two small drives | survive one drive failure ; Local scratch, dataset cache, image store, fast checkpoint staging | RAID 0 across NVMe or no RAID | maximum throughput, data is reproducible (orange: losing one drive loses the array) ; Valuable local data on a storage server | RAID 6 or 10, or erasure coding in Lustre, Ceph, GPFS | fault tolerance without a single controller as a point of failure ; Cloud | none, or RAID 0 of local SSDs | provider replicates the disk, local SSD is ephemeral. Green bar: for anything you cannot lose, choose a redundant level and keep a separate backup.
alt: A table matching RAID levels to the job a volume does on a GPU node.
cap: Match the RAID level to the job, and use RAID 0 only when the data can be rebuilt.

name: l13-multipath
title: Multipath: one LUN, several paths
spec: Left: a SAN LUN. Two HBAs and two switches giving four paths. Middle: OS sees four block devices sdb, sdc, sdd, sde (grey, component paths). Right: one green device built by multipathd, then LVM and filesystem on top. Rules in a list: build filesystems and LVM on the multipath device, never on a component path; exclude paths in the LVM filter; blacklist local disks and virtio disks. Monospace: multipath -ll.
alt: Several physical paths to one LUN appear as several block devices that multipath merges into one.
cap: Always build filesystems and LVM on the multipath device, never on a component path.

name: l14-grub-config
title: Never edit grub.cfg
spec: Left-to-right flow: /etc/default/grub (settings such as GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX) plus /etc/grub.d/ scripts (00_header, 10_linux, 30_os-prober, 40_custom) into the generator grub-mkconfig, labelled sudo update-grub on Debian and Ubuntu and sudo grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg on RHEL with BIOS, producing grub.cfg in /boot/grub/ (orange: generated, your edits are overwritten). After: reboot, then cat /proc/cmdline to verify. Note: the scripts run in user space to generate the file, GRUB never runs them at boot.
alt: Settings and scripts feed a generator that writes grub.cfg, which you should never edit by hand.
cap: grub.cfg is generated, so change /etc/default/grub or /etc/grub.d and regenerate.

name: l14-boot-symptoms
title: Boot symptom to likely cause
spec: Table with Symptom, Likely cause, First action. Rows: no bootable device | boot order or mode wrong, ESP or MBR damaged | efibootmgr, grub-install ; grub rescue> prompt | GRUB cannot find its prefix | ls, set prefix ; VFS: Unable to mount root fs on unknown-block(0,0) | no driver for root device or stale initramfs | boot older kernel, rebuild initramfs ; (initramfs) shell | root device not found in time | rootwait, check UUID ; emergency mode | fstab or fsck failed | journalctl -xb, fix /etc/fstab ; GPU missing after boot | DKMS failed or Secure Boot rejected module | dkms status, mokutil --sb-state. Footer: change one thing before you test again.
alt: A table that maps common boot symptoms to their likely cause and first action.
cap: Identify the failing boot stage first, then change only one thing before testing again.

name: l14-secure-boot
title: The Secure Boot trust chain
spec: Horizontal chain of boxes with arrows labelled verifies and runs: firmware (trusts vendor keys) then shim (Microsoft-signed) then GRUB then kernel then kernel modules. Beside the last box an orange callout: out-of-tree modules such as the NVIDIA driver built by DKMS must be signed, otherwise the kernel refuses with Required key not available or module verification failed and nvidia-smi fails. Below, three options: disable Secure Boot in firmware; enrol a MOK (mokutil --import) and sign modules; use distribution-signed or vendor-precompiled driver packages. Note: enrolment needs console interaction at next boot, so do it once in the image build.
alt: Each stage of the boot verifies the next, up to the kernel modules.
cap: A signed chain from firmware to kernel modules means an unsigned GPU driver module will not load.

name: l15-service-types
title: How systemd knows a service is started
spec: Table with Type=, Considered started when, Use. Rows: simple (default) | right after fork, process stays in foreground | modern foreground daemons ; exec | after exec() succeeds | catches missing binaries ; forking | parent exits, systemd tracks the child | traditional daemons ; oneshot | process runs to completion, often with RemainAfterExit=yes | setup tasks ; notify | service calls sd_notify("READY=1") | daemons with explicit readiness. Values in monospace. Footer: systemd tracks all processes with cgroups.
anchor: ### Service types: how systemd knows a service is "started"
alt: A table of Type= values and when systemd considers a service started.
cap: Type= tells systemd what the main process does at start-up and when the service counts as ready.

name: l15-socket-activation
title: Socket activation
spec: Timeline in three boxes. 1 systemd holds the socket (echo.socket, ListenStream=22222) while no service runs. 2 a client connects. 3 systemd starts the service (echo@.service) and hands it the connection. With Accept=true, systemd accepts each connection and starts a new instance named echo@<n>-... per connection. Orange note: ss -ltnp shows systemd as the listener, not the daemon. Unit names and options monospace. Link rule: echo.socket activates echo.service by name.
alt: systemd holds the listening socket and starts the service when a client connects.
cap: A rarely used service uses no resources until a client needs it.

name: l15-timer-pair
title: A timer and its service
spec: Two boxes joined by an arrow. Left: fstrim-data.timer with lines OnCalendar=Sun *-*-* 03:00:00 ; RandomizedDelaySec=30min ; Persistent=true ; AccuracySec=1min ; WantedBy=timers.target. Right: fstrim-data.service with Type=oneshot and ExecStart=/usr/sbin/fstrim -v /data. Arrow labelled activates. Orange chip: enable the timer, not the service: sudo systemctl enable --now fstrim-data.timer. Annotations: Persistent=true runs a missed job at next start; RandomizedDelaySec= spreads load. Two trigger families: calendar (OnCalendar=) and monotonic (OnBootSec=, OnUnitActiveSec=).
alt: A timer unit activates a oneshot service on a calendar schedule.
cap: A timer fires a matching service, and Persistent=true catches up a run missed while the machine was off.

name: l15-journalctl
title: Filtering the journal
spec: Grid of command chips, each with a short meaning: journalctl -b this boot (-b -1 previous boot); journalctl -u sshd by unit; journalctl -u kubelet -f follow; journalctl -k kernel messages; journalctl -p err priority err and worse; journalctl --since yesterday time window; journalctl -n 100 --no-pager last lines; journalctl --vacuum-size=2G trim old logs. Orange note: default Storage=auto writes to /var/log/journal only if that directory exists, otherwise in memory under /run/log/journal. Commands monospace.
alt: The most common journalctl filters by boot, unit, kernel, priority and time.
cap: Each journalctl option filters the journal in a different way.

name: l16-severity
title: Syslog severity levels
spec: Vertical ladder of eight rows from top to bottom: 0 emerg system unusable; 1 alert act immediately; 2 crit critical condition; 3 err error; 4 warning warning; 5 notice normal but significant; 6 info informational; 7 debug debug detail. Colour fading from orange at 0 to light green at 7. Left arrow labelled more urgent pointing up, right arrow less urgent pointing down. Side note: in the journal severity is called priority, field PRIORITY=, filter journalctl -p. Names monospace.
alt: Eight severity levels from emerg at 0 to debug at 7.
cap: A smaller severity number means a more urgent message.

name: l16-rotation-inode
title: Rotation and open log files
spec: Three steps left to right. 1 daemon writes to app.log (inode A). 2 logrotate renames app.log to app.log.1; the daemon still writes to the same inode, now under the new name (orange). 3 Fix: tell the daemon to reopen with SIGHUP (postrotate: systemctl kill -s HUP ...), or use copytruncate, which copies then truncates in place and may lose lines in the copy window. Footer: Linux tracks the open file, not its name. Also small config chips: daily, rotate 14, compress, delaycompress, missingok, notifempty. Test with sudo logrotate -d /etc/logrotate.d/slurm.
alt: Renaming a log does not move a process that holds it open, so the daemon must reopen it.
cap: A process keeps writing to the same inode after rename, so rotation needs a reopen or copytruncate.

name: l16-safe-cron
title: A safe cron job
spec: One monospace crontab line in the centre: */5 * * * * root flock -n /run/lock/gpu-health.lock timeout 120 /usr/local/bin/gpu-health.sh 2>&1 | logger -t gpu-health. Callouts: */5 * * * * every five minutes; flock -n prevents overlapping runs; timeout 120 kills a hang; logger -t gpu-health sends output to the journal. Header lines shown above: SHELL=/bin/bash, PATH=..., MAILTO="". Orange note: cron sets only HOME, LOGNAME, SHELL=/bin/sh and PATH=/usr/bin:/bin. Takeaway bar: before you schedule a job, make sure it is safe to run twice.
alt: A cron line wrapped with flock, timeout and logger guards.
cap: Guards against overlap, hangs and lost output make a cron job safe on a fleet.

name: l17-page-faults
title: Minor and major page faults
spec: Left: process with virtual memory; malloc(1<<30) consumes almost no RAM until pages are touched (demand paging). Two outcomes from a touch: minor fault (green): no I/O, new zero page or already-cached file page, cheap and frequent; major fault (orange): kernel must read from storage, first touch of uncached file page or swapping an anonymous page back in, slow. Bottom strip of size terms: VSZ or VIRT counts everything allocated; RSS only the part in RAM; PSS divides shared pages among users; USS unique set size.
anchor: ### Demand paging, page faults, memory states
alt: Touching a page triggers a cheap minor fault or a slow major fault that reads storage.
cap: Linux hands out virtual memory immediately and backs it with physical pages only when touched.

name: l17-overcommit
title: Overcommit modes
spec: Three cards for vm.overcommit_memory: 0 (default) heuristic, refuse only obviously excessive single requests; 1 always allow, never fail malloc; 2 strict, total committed memory limited to swap plus vm.overcommit_ratio% of RAM, allocations fail with ENOMEM (orange, the only hard limit). Below: flow for 0 and 1: malloc succeeds, memory runs out later at first touch, then the OOM killer picks a victim. Note: overcommit defers the failure.
alt: Three overcommit policies and when the failure shows up.
cap: Only mode 2 enforces a hard limit, while the others defer failure to first touch and the OOM killer.

name: l17-thp-modes
title: Huge pages: explicit versus transparent
spec: Two columns. Left, Explicit hugetlb: reserved in a dedicated pool (echo 1024 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/nr_hugepages is 2 GiB), not swappable, only apps that ask use it; 1 GiB pages need boot parameters; for VM guests, DPDK, RDMA, large in-memory databases. Right, Transparent THP: kernel backs large aligned anonymous regions with 2 MiB pages by itself; /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled has values always, madvise, never; training nodes always or madvise; latency-critical inference, databases, Redis madvise or never with defrag=defer (orange). Top note: huge pages shrink the page table and raise TLB reach.
anchor: ## 8. Huge pages and transparent huge pages
alt: Explicit huge pages are reserved in a pool, while transparent huge pages are used automatically by the kernel.
cap: THP is automatic and can add latency spikes, while explicit huge pages give a guaranteed page size.

name: l17-memory-policy
title: Memory policy by node type
spec: Table with columns Node type, Swap, Swappiness, THP, Limits. Rows: Training or HPC compute | none or minimal | 0 to 10 | always or madvise | cgroup memory.max per job, memlock unlimited ; Inference or latency-critical | none | 0 to 10 | madvise or never | per-service limits, memory.high as early warning ; Login or shared nodes | small swap, maybe zram | 10 to 60 | default | per-user slice MemoryMax ; Kubernetes workers | usually off | low | per workload | systemReserved, kubeReserved, QoS classes. Green bar: start from your row and change it only after you measure.
alt: A table of starting memory settings for training, inference, login and Kubernetes nodes.
cap: Start from the row for your node type and change it only after you measure.

name: l18-sched-classes
title: Scheduling classes
spec: Vertical stack, highest on top: Stop (kernel internal); Deadline SCHED_DEADLINE; Real-time SCHED_FIFO and SCHED_RR with priority 1 to 99 (orange: a busy real-time task starves everything below); Fair CFS/EEVDF SCHED_OTHER, SCHED_BATCH, SCHED_IDLE, the default for ordinary processes; Idle (runs when nothing else is runnable). Side chips monospace: chrt -p $$ ; sudo chrt -f 50 ./latency_task ; ps -eo pid,cls,rtprio,ni,pri,comm. Note: use real-time policies sparingly.
alt: Scheduling classes are ordered, with real-time tasks above all fair tasks.
cap: The real-time class sits above every fair task, which makes it powerful and dangerous.

name: l18-weight-quota
title: Weight versus quota
spec: Two panels. Left Weight (cpu.weight, 1 to 10000, default 100; v1 cpu.shares default 1024): a promise about proportions, only under contention and only among siblings, never wastes capacity, never limits alone; Kubernetes CPU request becomes weight. Right Quota (cpu.max, form $MAX $PERIOD in microseconds, default max 100000): hard ceiling; 200000 100000 means 200 ms of CPU per 100 ms period, two CPUs' worth. Example orange: 16 busy threads with a 2-CPU quota burn 200 ms in about 12.5 ms then sleep 87.5 ms. Check throttling: nr_throttled versus nr_periods in cpu.stat.
anchor: ## 7. The CPU controller: weight, quota and throttling
alt: Weight shares CPU proportionally under contention, while quota sets a hard ceiling.
cap: A weight is a proportion that only matters under contention, but a quota is a ceiling that always applies.

name: l18-isolation
title: Keeping kernel and others off chosen cores
spec: Left: grid of eight CPUs, cores 0-1 labelled housekeeping and cores 2-15 labelled isolated (orange) for the data loader. Right: mechanism list in monospace with effect: isolcpus=2-15 scheduler does not place tasks there unless pinned ; nohz_full=2-15 stop the periodic tick ; rcu_nocbs=2-15 offload RCU callbacks ; irqaffinity=0-1 IRQs to housekeeping CPUs ; systemd CPUAffinity= confine services ; cpuset.cpus.partition=isolated at runtime. Note: most are boot parameters; the cpuset row works without reboot.
anchor: ### Isolation: keeping the kernel and others off chosen cores
alt: Boot and runtime settings that keep the kernel, interrupts and other tasks off chosen CPUs.
cap: Isolation keeps the rest of the system off the cores you reserve for latency-sensitive work.

name: l18-cgroup-v1-v2
title: cgroups v1 versus v2
spec: Two panels. Left v1: separate trees per controller (/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/, /memory/, /blkio/), a process can sit in a different group in each tree. Right v2: one unified tree, a process is in exactly one cgroup, one cgroup2 mount at /sys/fs/cgroup; no internal processes rule: only leaf groups hold processes; controllers enabled by writing +cpu +memory to cgroup.subtree_control. Bottom commands monospace: stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup/ (cgroup2fs means pure v2; tmpfs means v1 or hybrid) ; cat /proc/self/cgroup. v2 in green as default.
alt: Version 1 uses one tree per controller, and version 2 uses a single unified tree.
cap: In v2 every process belongs to exactly one cgroup in a single hierarchy.

name: l19-ns-syscalls
title: Three system calls for namespaces
spec: Three columns. clone(2) creates a new process, optionally in new namespaces via CLONE_NEW* flags, used by runtimes to start a container's first process. unshare(2) moves the calling process into new namespaces, for PID only future children enter; wrapped by the unshare command. setns(2) joins an existing namespace through a file descriptor from /proc/PID/ns/*; wrapped by nsenter; docker exec and kubectl exec are setns then exec. Bottom strip: a namespace lives while a process, an open file descriptor to /proc/PID/ns/xxx, or a bind mount refers to it. Names monospace.
alt: The clone, unshare and setns calls create or join namespaces.
cap: Three system calls do all the namespace work: create with clone, move with unshare and join with setns.

name: l19-mount-propagation
title: Mount propagation
spec: Four small cards between a host mount and a namespace mount with arrows showing event direction: shared sends and receives events; slave only receives; private neither; unbindable private and cannot be bind-mounted. Orange warning: systemd makes / shared by default, so a naive new mount namespace can leak mounts back to the host; runtimes remount root as rslave or rprivate first. Command chip: findmnt -o TARGET,PROPAGATION.
alt: Mount propagation flags control whether mount events pass between namespaces.
cap: A shared mount can leak events back to the host, so runtimes make the root private or slave first.

name: l19-chroot-pivot
title: chroot versus pivot_root
spec: Two panels. Left chroot(2): changes a process's root directory, the old root can stay reachable through open file descriptors, not a security boundary (orange). Right pivot_root(2): used by container runtimes inside a mount namespace, swaps the root mount so the old root can be unmounted and detached completely (green). Tiny sequence under right panel: new mount namespace, make mounts private, bind-mount new rootfs onto itself, mount proc, sysfs and tmpfs, pivot_root.
alt: chroot only changes the visible root, while pivot_root swaps the root mount and detaches the old one.
cap: Container runtimes use pivot_root because chroot is not a security boundary.

name: l19-isolation-compare
title: Containers, VMs and lighter options
spec: Table with columns Hardware VM (KVM/QEMU), Container, MicroVM (Firecracker, Kata), gVisor. Rows: Kernel | own guest | shared host | own minimal guest | Go kernel intercepting syscalls ; Isolation | strong | weaker | strong | medium ; Start time | seconds | milliseconds | about 100 to 200 ms | milliseconds ; GPU access | passthrough or vGPU/MIG | native driver via device nodes (orange) | possible but complex | limited. Takeaway bar: decide early whether the isolation needs a hardware boundary.
alt: A comparison of VMs, containers, microVMs and gVisor on kernel, isolation, start time and GPU access.
cap: A container uses the native GPU driver through device nodes, while a VM needs passthrough or vGPU.

name: l20-build-ladder
title: What each step adds
spec: Vertical ladder of steps, each a box with what it adds: Step 1 root filesystem (base); Step 2 plain chroot, only a different filesystem view; Step 3 unshare with PID, mount, UTS, IPC and net namespaces; Step 4 OverlayFS layers plus pivot_root; Step 5 cgroup limits for CPU, memory and PIDs; Step 6 veth pair, bridge and NAT; Step 7 drop privileges. Right column of the real-container check Step 8 compare with docker run, orange. Commands monospace: chroot, unshare, pivot_root, cgroup.
alt: The lab builds a container by adding a filesystem, namespaces, layers, limits, networking and reduced privilege.
cap: Each step adds one kernel feature until the result matches a real container.

name: l20-lab-network
title: Lab network: bridge, veth and NAT
spec: Diagram. Host box containing bridge br-lab with IP 10.77.0.1/24. A veth pair: vethh0 on the host attached to br-lab, vethc0 moved into the container network namespace and renamed eth0 with 10.77.0.2/24 and default route via 10.77.0.1. Host uplink on the right via iptables NAT rule MASQUERADE for 10.77.0.0/24 to the Internet. Commands monospace: ip link add vethh0 type veth peer name vethc0 ; sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1. Test: ping -c2 10.77.0.1 and ping -c2 8.8.8.8.
alt: A bridge, a veth pair and a NAT rule connect the container namespace to the host and the Internet.
cap: One end of the veth pair stays on the host bridge and the other becomes eth0 inside the container.

name: l20-enter-sh
title: Inside enter.sh
spec: Numbered vertical flow of the script's actions: mount --make-rprivate /; bind-mount /lab/merged onto itself; cd /lab/merged; mount proc, sysfs (read-only), tmpfs for dev, mknod for null, zero, urandom, tty; mount tmpfs on tmp; pivot_root . oldroot; umount -l /oldroot and rmdir; hostname container1; exec /bin/sh. Top box above flow: overlay mount lowerdir=/lab/base, upperdir=/lab/upper, workdir=/lab/work onto /lab/merged. Orange highlight on pivot_root. Commands monospace.
anchor: ## Step 4. Layers with OverlayFS and a proper root switch
alt: The overlay mount and the enter.sh steps that switch the container's root with pivot_root.
cap: The script makes mounts private, builds the root, pivots into it and detaches the old root.

name: l21-cap-sets
title: The five capability sets
spec: Five stacked boxes with one-line roles: Permitted (upper bound of what the thread may hold in its effective set); Effective (what the kernel checks right now, highlighted orange); Inheritable (may be passed across execve); Bounding (limit on what can ever be gained through execve, dropping is irreversible for the process tree); Ambient (kept across execve of non-privileged programs). Right side monospace commands: grep Cap /proc/self/status (CapInh CapPrm CapEff CapBnd CapAmb) ; capsh --decode=... ; sudo setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep /usr/local/bin/myserver.
alt: The five capability sets of a thread and what each one does.
cap: The effective set is what the kernel checks, and dropping from the bounding set cannot be undone.

name: l21-seccomp
title: seccomp filters system calls
spec: Flow: program calls a system call, then a seccomp filter checks it, then allowed goes to the kernel (green) and blocked is refused (orange, examples mount, kexec_load, init_module, reboot). Notes: filters are inherited by children and cannot be removed; stacked filters, the most restrictive result wins; unprivileged process must set no_new_privs first. Monospace check: grep -E 'Seccomp|NoNewPrivs' /proc/self/status with Seccomp: 0 none, 1 strict, 2 filter. Kubernetes: seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault.
alt: A seccomp filter decides call by call which system calls reach the kernel.
cap: seccomp refuses system calls the service never needed, and filters cannot be removed once installed.

name: l21-ssh-hardening
title: SSH hardening choices
spec: Left column: key settings from the drop-in file /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-hardening.conf as monospace chips: PermitRootLogin no ; PasswordAuthentication no ; PubkeyAuthentication yes ; AuthenticationMethods publickey ; AllowGroups ssh-users hpc-users ; MaxAuthTries 3 ; AllowAgentForwarding no ; AllowTcpForwarding no ; LogLevel VERBOSE. Right: Match Group hpc-users with AllowTcpForwarding yes (orange: enabled for that group only). Bottom flow: sudo sshd -t, reload, keep an existing session open while testing. Also bastion: ssh -J bastion node01.
alt: Key sshd settings, a per-group Match exception and the safe way to test them.
cap: Disable passwords and root login, allow specific groups, validate with sshd -t and keep a session open.

name: l22-module-config
title: Two files for modules
spec: Two boxes. Left /etc/modules-load.d/gpu.conf lists what to load at boot (nvidia, nvidia_uvm, nvidia_peermem), read by systemd-modules-load. Right /etc/modprobe.d/nvidia.conf sets options and policy, read by modprobe: options nvidia ..., blacklist nouveau. Below: blacklist only stops automatic loading via aliases; stronger form install nouveau /bin/false (orange). Check merged result: sudo modprobe -c | grep -i nvidia and systemd-analyze cat-config modprobe.d. Note: modules needed to mount root or reach the network must be in the initramfs.
alt: One file chooses which modules load at boot and another sets their options and blacklist.
cap: modules-load.d lists what to load, and modprobe.d sets how and whether it loads.

name: l22-driver-delivery
title: Four ways to deliver a GPU driver
spec: Table with Approach, Pros, Cons. Rows: Precompiled kmod packages | no compiler on nodes, deterministic | tied to supported kernel list ; Golden image (Packer plus Ansible) | reproducible, rollback is the previous image, fits PXE | needs an image pipeline ; GPU Operator driver container | Kubernetes-native lifecycle | needs the node's kernel and headers available ; DKMS on nodes (orange) | easy on a workstation or tiny cluster | fragile at scale. Takeaway bar: compile the driver once in CI against a pinned kernel and never compile on a compute node.
anchor: ### Why large fleets avoid compiling on nodes
alt: A comparison of precompiled packages, golden images, the GPU Operator driver container and DKMS on nodes.
cap: Large fleets compile once in CI against a pinned kernel instead of compiling on compute nodes.

name: l22-upgrade-steps
title: Safe driver upgrade on one node
spec: Seven numbered boxes in a vertical flow: 1 cordon and drain; 2 stop GPU consumers (DCGM, Fabric Manager, persistence daemon); 3 install new driver packages with matching Fabric Manager, toolkit, MOFED/DOCA; 4 verify the module build for the target kernel (dkms status); 5 reboot; 6 validate (nvidia-smi, nvidia-smi topo -m, dcgmi diag -r 2, single-node NCCL test); 7 uncordon, roll out in waves, keep previous image for rollback. Orange highlight on step 4. Commands monospace.
alt: Seven steps to upgrade a GPU driver on one node before touching the fleet.
cap: Cordon, upgrade, verify the build for the target kernel, reboot, validate, then uncordon and roll out in waves.

name: l22-sysctl-persist
title: sysctl: runtime versus persistent
spec: Two paths from a command. Top path orange: sudo sysctl -w vm.swappiness=1 changes /proc/sys/vm/swappiness immediately, lost after reboot. Bottom path green: write 'vm.swappiness = 1' into /etc/sysctl.d/90-gpu.conf, then sudo sysctl --system reloads all files. Name mapping: vm.swappiness corresponds to /proc/sys/vm/swappiness. Side notes: some keys exist only after a module loads (net.bridge.* needs br_netfilter); many network keys are per net namespace. Check: systemd-analyze cat-config sysctl.d.
alt: A sysctl -w change is runtime only, while a file under /etc/sysctl.d persists across reboots.
cap: Use sysctl -w to test and a sysctl.d file to make the setting survive a reboot.

name: l23-latency-scale
title: Latency scaled to human time
spec: Ladder table with Event, Typical latency, Scaled. Rows: CPU cycle 0.3 ns = 1 s ; L1 cache 1 ns = 3 s ; L2 cache 3 ns = 10 s ; L3 cache 10 ns = 33 s ; DRAM 100 ns = 6 minutes ; NVMe / flash I/O 10 to 100 µs = 9 to 90 hours ; Rotational disk I/O 1 to 10 ms = 1 to 12 months ; Cross-continent network (SF to NY) 40 ms = 4 years ; TCP retransmit timeout 1 to 3 s = centuries ; Physical server reboot minutes = tens of millennia. Orange on DRAM and cross-continent rows. Takeaway: a 10 µs disk read is really a cache hit, not a disk.
alt: Typical latencies scaled so that one CPU cycle takes one second.
cap: Scaling latencies to human time shows how large the gaps between memory, disk and network are.

name: l23-mantras
title: Performance mantras
spec: Seven steps as a descending staircase from most effective to least: 1 Don't do it. 2 Do it, but don't do it again. 3 Do it less. 4 Do it later. 5 Do it when they're not looking. 6 Do it concurrently. 7 Do it more cheaply. Orange highlight on step 1. Arrow at the side labelled order of effectiveness for fixes.
alt: The performance mantras ranked from most to least effective.
cap: The order of the mantras is the point: eliminating work beats making it cheaper.

name: l23-workload-4q
title: Characterise the load first
spec: Four boxes around a central box 'the load (input, not performance)': Who is causing the load (user, job, tenant, client IP, process); Why is it issued (code path, stack trace, API, dataset); What are its characteristics (IOPS, bytes, read/write mix, request size, batch size, include variance); How does it change over time (daily pattern, ramp, bursts, per epoch). Orange note: an unexpected client may be an attack, a mis-deployed cron job or a runaway retry loop.
alt: Four questions about who, why, what and when characterise the load before measuring speed.
cap: Characterise the input load, not the resulting performance.

name: l23-ai-metrics
title: AI efficiency metrics
spec: Table with Metric and Definition. Rows: Throughput | tokens/s or samples/s per GPU and aggregate ; Step time breakdown | data wait, H2D, forward, backward, communication, optimizer, checkpoint ; MFU | achieved model FLOPs/s divided by peak hardware FLOPs/s ; Scaling efficiency | throughput(N) divided by N times throughput(1) ; Goodput | fraction of time making forward training progress ; GPU idle gaps (bubbles) | time between kernels or collectives ; Inference | TTFT, TPOT, p99, tokens/s/GPU. Green bar: start with throughput and the step-time breakdown before you tune anything else.
alt: Outcome metrics that measure work delivered, such as throughput, MFU, scaling efficiency and goodput.
cap: Use outcome metrics rather than raw utilisation because they measure work delivered.

name: l24-tool-matrix
title: Which kind of tool
spec: Two-by-three matrix. Columns System-wide and Per-process. Rows Counters, Profiling (sampling), Tracing (every event). Cells in monospace: Counters: vmstat, mpstat, iostat, sar | ps, top, pidstat, /proc/PID/* ; Profiling: perf record, perf top | py-spy, gprof, cProfile ; Tracing: perf trace, Ftrace, bpftrace, tcpdump | strace, ltrace, gdb. Side note: counters are like an odometer, read twice; profiling is a camera taking one photo per interval, e.g. 99 Hz; tracing records every event so overhead grows with the event rate (orange).
alt: Tools sorted by system-wide versus per-process scope and by counting, sampling or tracing.
cap: Two questions sort the tools: whole system or one process, and counting, sampling or tracing.

name: l24-perf-workflow
title: Count first, then record
spec: Three-step arrow flow. 1 perf stat: cheap counting, gives IPC (an insn per cycle below about 0.5 suggests memory stalls), e.g. sudo perf stat -a -- sleep 5. 2 perf record: sampling profile, e.g. sudo perf record -F 99 -a -g -- sleep 30. 3 perf report --stdio -n or perf script, or turn into a flame graph. Orange note under step 2: binaries built without frame pointers show broken stacks; Python shows interpreter frames unless python -X perf or py-spy. Commands monospace.
alt: Counting with perf stat comes first, then sampling with perf record, then reporting.
cap: Run perf stat first because counting is cheap, then record and report only where it matters.

name: l24-bpftrace-timing
title: bpftrace entry and return timing
spec: Top: probe shape in monospace: probe[,probe...] /filter/ { action; }. Below, a two-probe diagram: kprobe:vfs_read stores @start[tid] = nsecs; kretprobe:vfs_read with filter /@start[tid]/ computes $duration_us = (nsecs - @start[tid]) / 1000, adds to @us = hist($duration_us), then delete(@start[tid]). Arrow between probes labelled map keyed by thread ID. Output: a latency histogram in microseconds. Green bar: entry probe stores a timestamp, return probe computes the delta and aggregates in a histogram.
alt: An entry probe stores a timestamp by thread ID and a return probe turns it into a histogram.
cap: The filter on the return probe protects against calls that began before tracing started.

name: l24-overhead-rules
title: Tracing overhead rules
spec: Left: scale bar for event rate: under about 10k events per second is negligible; above about 100k per second needs care; scheduler, memory allocation, network packet and syscall events can exceed 1M per second (orange). Right: preference ladder tracepoints, then kprobes, then uprobes (every uprobe hit traps into the kernel; avoid on malloc, memcpy, CUDA launch paths). Bottom rules: count first with perf stat -e event -a sleep 1; aggregate in kernel with maps and histograms; filter on PID, cgroup, comm; keep durations short.
alt: Event-rate thresholds and probe-type preferences that keep tracing overhead safe.
cap: Count the event rate first and prefer tracepoints over kprobes over uprobes.

name: l25-six-questions
title: Six questions for every result
spec: Six numbered boxes in two rows of three: 1 Why not double? What is the limiter; 2 Did it break limits? check against known maxima; 3 Did it error? errors skew results; 4 Does it reproduce? repeat, look at variation, test other instances; 5 Does it matter? is the workload relevant to production; 6 Did it even happen? was the operation performed rather than blocked, cached or optimised away. Green bar: a number you cannot answer these questions about is a hypothesis, not a result.
alt: Six questions to ask of any benchmark result before accepting it.
cap: Each question catches a different way a benchmark result can mislead you.

name: l25-ramp-knee
title: Ramping load and the knee
spec: Chart with load on the x axis (clients, threads or QPS added in steps). Two curves: throughput rising then flattening, latency percentiles flat then bending upward. Mark the knee where the curve bends in orange. Label: report the highest load with acceptable latency, not the highest throughput. Note: hold each level long enough to settle.
alt: Throughput and latency plotted against stepped load, with the knee marked.
cap: The result is the highest load whose latency is still acceptable, not the highest throughput.

name: l25-sanity-math
title: Sanity-check arithmetic
spec: Worked rows: Claim 50,000 NFS IOPS of 8 KiB over one 1 GbE link: 50,000 x 8 KiB = 400,000 KB/s, about 3.2 Gbit/s, more than 1 Gbit/s, verdict impossible, client cache measured (orange). Claim 350 MB/s over 1 GbE: 350 x 8 = 2.8 Gbit/s, bogus, about 119 MB/s is the real ceiling. Claim 400 Gb/s NIC delivers 55 GB/s per direction: 400 Gb/s = 50 GB/s raw, above line rate. Footer: check bits against bytes, GiB against GB, one direction against both, per GPU against aggregate.
anchor: ### Sanity-check arithmetic you should do instantly
alt: Quick arithmetic shows when a claimed number exceeds a physical limit.
cap: Do the arithmetic with units and treat any number above a physical limit as a measurement error.

name: l25-passive-active
title: Passive versus active benchmarking
spec: Two panels. Left Passive (anti-method, orange): run the tool with various options, make slides, hand over; results may be buggy or limited by the tool or an unrelated component such as a congested network or a single thread. Right Active (core method, green): analyse the system with observability tools while the benchmark runs, to confirm what is tested and what limits it. Example below: throughput plateaus at 700 samples/s while server resources are idle, so check the load generator, which was single-threaded.
alt: Passive benchmarking reads a report afterwards, while active benchmarking watches the system during the run.
cap: Active benchmarking confirms what is tested and what limits it while the benchmark runs.

name: l26-memory-translation
title: Two translation stages
spec: Chain of three address boxes: guest virtual, guest physical, host physical, with arrows labelled guest page tables and host mapping. Below two approaches side by side: Shadow page tables (older): hypervisor intercepts every guest page-table change, keeps combined guest-virtual to host-physical tables, many exits. Nested paging (EPT on Intel, NPT on AMD): hardware walks both tables, a two-dimensional page walk, fewer exits (green) but a TLB miss costs more memory reads (orange: worst case 24 reads with 4-level paging in both dimensions, 8 with 1 GiB huge pages in both guest and host).
alt: A guest address is translated twice, by shadow page tables or by hardware nested paging.
cap: Nested paging cuts exits but makes each TLB miss more expensive, which is why huge pages help.

name: l26-vm-net-modes
title: VM networking modes
spec: Table with Mode, How, Use. Rows: User-mode (SLIRP) | QEMU NAT with port forwarding | quick tests, slow ; libvirt NAT network (default) | virbr0 bridge, dnsmasq, NAT, guests on 192.168.122.0/24 | dev and test, not reachable from outside ; Linux bridge | tap devices on host bridge br0 enslaving the NIC | servers that must be reachable ; macvtap | virtual interface on a physical NIC | simple ; Open vSwitch | programmable switch | cloud-scale SDN ; SR-IOV VF or NIC passthrough | VF or PF into the guest | near-native throughput including RDMA. Takeaway bar: decide the network mode first, it determines who can reach the guest.
alt: The common VM networking modes and when to use each.
cap: Choose the network mode by asking who needs to reach the guest.

name: l26-cloud-init
title: Making a VM from a cloud image
spec: Left-to-right flow: base cloud image (jammy-server-cloudimg-amd64.img) then qemu-img create -f qcow2 -b ... vm1.qcow2 40G (thin copy-on-write overlay) ; user-data plus meta-data then cloud-localds seed.iso ; both into virt-install --name vm1 --import ; first boot cloud-init configures the instance ; virsh domifaddr vm1 then ssh ubuntu@<ip>. Orange note: no installer runs, which is why a new VM takes seconds. Commands monospace.
anchor: ### Creating a VM with a cloud image and cloud-init
alt: A thin overlay on a cloud image plus a cloud-init seed lets a new VM boot configured in seconds.
cap: A cloud image needs no installer because cloud-init configures it at first boot.

name: l26-tuning-order
title: Tuning order: host first
spec: Six numbered boxes in a ladder from the bottom: 1 Host (BIOS VT-x and VT-d, intel_iommu=on iommu=pt, performance governor); 2 CPU (host-passthrough, vcpupin on one NUMA node); 3 Memory (hugepages, locked, numatune strict); 4 Disk (virtio with iothreads, cache=none); 5 Network (virtio-net with vhost and multiqueue, correct MTU); 6 Guest (virtio drivers, qemu-guest-agent, tuned-adm). Orange on step 1. Takeaway bar: start with the host, because guest settings depend on what the host exposes.
anchor: ## 6. Performance: what costs what, and how to tune
alt: Six layers of VM tuning, from the host up to the guest.
cap: Tune the host first, then libvirt, then the guest.

name: l27-cloud-gpu-diffs
title: Why a cloud GPU node differs
spec: Four boxes around a centre box 'cloud GPU node': Noisy neighbours (shared CPU caches, memory bandwidth, NIC; shows as %steal and latency outliers); Virtual topology (the NUMA layout and PCIe tree the provider presents; flat view stops NCCL choosing best paths); Passthrough and SR-IOV (whole GPU passed through, NIC as virtual function; provider sets bandwidth caps, MTU, counters); Nested virtualisation (two layers of exits; often disabled on GPU types). Green bar: if a workload is slower in the cloud, check these four before you blame the software.
anchor: ### Why a cloud GPU node behaves differently
alt: Noisy neighbours, virtual topology, passthrough limits and nested virtualisation explain most cloud surprises.
cap: Check these four differences before blaming the software for a slower cloud GPU node.

name: l27-gpu-options
title: Where to run a GPU workload
spec: Table with Option, Pro, Con. Rows: GPU VM with passthrough | provisioning API, snapshots, tenant isolation, near-native GPU | hypervisor overhead on I/O unless offloaded ; Bare-metal instances | full topology and NIC/GPU control, no hypervisor, InfiniBand | longer provisioning, you own more of the stack ; Containers on VMs or bare metal | fast start, reproducibility | shared kernel, visibility limits ; MIG / vGPU slices | many small tenants on one GPU | no NCCL across MIG instances ; MicroVMs/Kata | strong isolation | GPU support complexity. Orange mark on Containers: almost all AI workloads run on top of one of the others.
anchor: ### VM, bare metal or container for GPUs?
alt: Five ways to run GPU workloads compared by their pros and cons.
cap: Each option trades control for convenience, so read the cons column as carefully as the pros.

name: l27-limits-use
title: Software limits under USE
spec: Table with Resource, Utilisation, Saturation. Rows: CPU quota | cpu.stat usage_usec vs cpu.max | nr_throttled, throttled_usec, PSI cpu ; Memory limit | memory.current vs memory.max | memory.events (high, max), PSI memory; errors oom_kill, exit 137 ; Disk I/O limit | io.stat vs io.max | io.pressure, latency growth ; PIDs | pids.current vs pids.max | fork failures, Resource temporarily unavailable ; VM vCPUs | guest CPU utilisation | %steal, run queue. Orange note: utilisation is measured against the limit, not against the physical resource. Names monospace.
anchor: ## 5. Resource controls under the USE method
alt: Each software limit paired with the signals that show whether it is binding.
cap: Utilisation is measured against the limit, not the physical resource, which is what makes the table useful in a shared cloud.

name: l28-topo-codes
title: Reading nvidia-smi topo -m
spec: Distance ladder from closest to farthest, each a labelled box: X self; NV# NVLink with # links; PIX path crosses at most one PCIe bridge (green, best for GPUDirect RDMA with PXB); PXB crosses multiple PCIe bridges; PHB goes through a PCIe host bridge, the CPU root complex; NODE crosses PCIe host bridges within one NUMA node; SYS crosses NUMA nodes through the inter-socket link (orange, avoid between a worker's CPU, GPU and NIC). Monospace command nvidia-smi topo -m. Takeaway bar: aim for GPU and NIC pairs at PIX or PXB.
alt: The connection codes in nvidia-smi topo -m ordered by distance.
cap: Each topology code is a statement about distance, and SYS between a worker's CPU, GPU and NIC should be avoided.

name: l28-k8s-mechanisms
title: Kubernetes knobs for a tuned node
spec: Table with Concern then Mechanism. Rows: GPU allocation | NVIDIA device plugin (nvidia.com/gpu), GPU Operator ; CPU pinning | cpuManagerPolicy: static, Guaranteed pods with integer CPU requests ; NUMA alignment | topologyManagerPolicy: single-numa-node ; Reserved cores | reservedSystemCPUs, kubeReserved, systemReserved ; Memory | Guaranteed QoS, requests equal limits ; Network | hostNetwork or Multus plus SR-IOV/RDMA device plugin ; I/O isolation | not native, use node-level cgroup v2 io.max ; Jitter (orange) | homogeneous workloads per node, dedicate whole nodes. Names monospace.
alt: A map from each tuning concern to the Kubernetes setting that implements it.
cap: Kubernetes expresses the same tuning ideas through its own knobs, and dedicating whole nodes removes jitter.

name: l28-fleet-checks
title: Fleet health checks to automate
spec: Four layered boxes: 1 Boot-time audit (topology, links, settings, versions; fails closed so a failing node stays drained); 2 Prolog and epilog (GPUs visible and healthy, ECC clean, no Xid since last job, clocks nominal, no leftover processes); 3 Periodic checks (dcgmi diag -r 1 often, -r 2 or -r 3 on a schedule, nccl-tests pair and ring tests); 4 Statistical outlier detection (compare reference-step time, NCCL busbw, GPU clocks, temperatures with the fleet median; flag beyond 3 MAD, orange). Commands monospace.
alt: Four automated checks from boot audit to statistical outlier detection.
cap: Stragglers are the expensive failure, so compare each node against the fleet median.

name: l28-troubleshoot
title: Symptom to first check
spec: Table with Symptom, Likely cause, First check. Rows: One rank slower than others | thermal or power throttling, PCIe downtrain | nvidia-smi -q -d PERFORMANCE,CLOCK,POWER ; Run-to-run variance | THP, NUMA balancing, C-states, IRQs on training cores | perf sched, mpstat ; Low NCCL bandwidth | wrong NIC/GPU affinity, fallback to TCP | NCCL_DEBUG=INFO, nvidia-smi topo -m ; DataLoader stalls | remote NUMA, too few workers, slow FS | iostat, pidstat ; OOM kill in a long job | limit counted pinned or cache | memory.events, dmesg ; Fleet differs after update | image, GRUB, sysctl or driver drift | run audit, diff against baseline. Commands monospace.
alt: A short troubleshooting map from symptoms to likely causes and first checks.
cap: Match the symptom to the row and run its first checks before exploring other causes.

name: l29-two-crypto
title: Two kinds of cryptography in SSH
spec: Two columns. Left Asymmetric (public-key): a key pair, what one key encrypts only the other can decrypt, used for identity and key exchange, slower. Right Symmetric: one shared secret key encrypts and decrypts, fast so it carries the bulk of the data, key replaced periodically during a long connection (limits data per key). Middle arrow: Diffie-Hellman family key exchange sets up the shared key. Bottom: server has a host key pair; client shows its fingerprint on first connection; save and restore /etc/ssh/ssh_host_* when reimaging. Monospace names.
alt: Public-key cryptography handles identity and key exchange, and symmetric encryption protects the session.
cap: SSH uses each kind of cryptography for the job it does best.

name: l29-forwarding-kinds
title: Four kinds of forwarding
spec: Four cards. Environment variables: SendEnv LANG LC_* on the client and AcceptEnv LANG LC_* on the server, both must agree. Port forwarding: ssh -L 8080:192.168.0.10:80 your.server.address then browse localhost:8080. X11 forwarding: remote graphical program displays on your local X server, needs xauth on both ends. Agent forwarding (orange): exposes your local agent, not the keys, anyone with root on that machine can use it while you are connected, prefer ProxyJump. Top note: everything travels inside the single encrypted SSH connection.
anchor: ## 5. Forwarding: environment, ports, X11 and agent
alt: Environment, port, X11 and agent forwarding all ride inside one SSH connection.
cap: Forwarding sends extra traffic through the single encrypted SSH connection.

name: l29-restricted-key
title: Restricting a key
spec: One long monospace authorized_keys line: from="10.0.0.0/8",command="/usr/local/bin/status-only",no-port-forwarding,no-pty ssh-ed25519 AAAA... monitor@mgmt. Callouts: from works only from the management subnet; command runs only one command; no-port-forwarding; no-pty; the key itself at the end. Green bar: give monitoring a narrow capability instead of a shell.
anchor: ### Restrict what a key may do
alt: Options placed before a key in authorized_keys limit where it may connect from and what it may run.
cap: A key limited to one command from one subnet is worth far less to an attacker than a general key.

name: l29-ipmi-tools
title: Managing the machine behind the machine
spec: Layer diagram. Bottom: BMC (management controller) with its own network access, works when the main system is hung or powered off. Above it four tool chips in monospace: ipmitool (lan print, sdr list, sol activate; leave with ~. or ~~. inside SSH); sol (serial-over-LAN, needs a getty on the serial port); conman (keeps many consoles open and logged); powerman (power control, no consoles). Side: modules ipmi_devintf, ipmi_si, ipmi_msghandler for the local controller. Orange security box: put controllers on a dedicated management network or VLAN, never expose a BMC to the internet.
anchor: ## 10. IPMI: managing the machine behind the machine
alt: The BMC with the tools used to reach its console, sensors and power control.
cap: IPMI reaches the hardware even when the operating system is down, so isolate it on a management network.

name: l30-tool-choice
title: Which tool for which job
spec: Table with You want to and Use. Rows: temporarily make files available on a trusted network | python3 -m http.server ; copy files across machines, repeatedly | rsync over SSH ; share regularly with Windows | Samba (SMB) ; mount Windows shares on Linux | mount -t cifs ; small-scale sharing between Linux machines, minimal setup | SSHFS ; larger filesystems from a NAS or server | NFS ; cloud storage | FUSE-based filesystems or the provider's CLI. Three group brackets: temporary and regular copying; Windows sharing; Linux-to-Linux and cloud. Orange note: large-scale sharing between many locations and users is not covered by this table.
alt: A table matching each sharing or copying job to the tool that fits it.
cap: Start with the job, not the tool.

name: l30-rsync-decide
title: How rsync decides what to send
spec: Flow: source and destination compared by quick check: size and modification time. Match then skip (green); different then send only the changed blocks. Side table of safeguards in monospace: -c checksum (slower, thorough); --ignore-existing; -b backup; -u skip files newer at destination; -P partial plus progress. Orange note: a second rsync -av should list nothing, but the quick check trusts two numbers, so use -c for data you cannot rebuild. Dry run: rsync -nva dir host:dest_dir.
alt: rsync skips files whose size and time match and offers options for stronger checks and safeguards.
cap: The quick check is cheap but trusts only size and time, so use checksums for data you cannot rebuild.

name: l30-stream-vs-random
title: Streamed file versus random access
spec: Two lanes over a network link between client and server. Top lane green: a video player reads one large file in order, the server can read ahead and buffer, fast. Bottom lane orange: a build opens thousands of small source files one after another, every open is a separate request that the server must accept, decode, find and load, so latency repeats, slow. Rule bar: large data without frequent random access can stay on the share; reading millions of small files, keep a local copy or stage the data.
anchor: ### Why a streamed file is fast and random access is slow
alt: Sequential reads of a large file are fast over a network, while many small random opens repeat the latency.
cap: The latency of each new file access is what makes network storage slow for many small files.

name: l30-remote-display
title: When X is too slow
spec: Table with Tool and Key note. Rows: VNC (TigerVNC) | very common, scaling and compression, any X application works, not multi-user: everyone sees one user's desktop (orange) ; RDP | Windows remote desktop, simultaneous users, closed protocol, Linux servers rare ; x2go | open, derived from NoMachine NX, no separate server service, connects over SSH ; NoMachine NX | commercial origin, free server allows two simultaneous users ; SPICE | another remote display protocol, less widespread. Top note: these send compressed images of the screen instead of drawing commands. Green bar: for Jupyter and TensorBoard, run the service on the node and tunnel its port over SSH.
anchor: ### When X is too slow: alternatives
alt: Remote display alternatives to X compared by their key limits.
cap: The alternatives send compressed screen images, and web UIs usually need only an SSH tunnel.
